extracted.intended_audience: fiction authors and storytellers aiming to write culturally diverse characters
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for authors on how to create culturally appropriate, non-stereotypical diverse characters in fiction, including research practices, intersectionality, and characterization techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead With Why
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure a character's demographic traits are included because the story or the character's role genuinely requires them, not to fill a stereotype or to add representational padding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inserting a character solely to mock, fulfill a stereotype, or superficially 'pad' diversity. Prefer either (a) writing a character whose background is essential to who they are and to the plot, or (b) creating a world where diverse demographic detail is normalized and treated like any other descriptive detail (names, hair color). Examples: Bad — Hawk in the Spenser novels (magical negro: a character who exists because his white friend needs him). Good — The Murderbot Diaries (diverse world where demographic details are incidental). Watch for anti-patterns like making a character a 'kindly math tutor asian' or 'greedy pawn shop owner jewish' simply to fit a stereotype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do Proper Research
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoroughly research cultures and identities you are depicting so you understand both visible traits and the deeper assumptions, experiences, and expectations that shape behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read widely (fiction, nonfiction, biographies) by and about members of the culture; immerse yourself in cultural outputs (art openings, plays, films, festivals) and observe behavior and social norms; travel to different places when possible to gain perspective on your own cultural assumptions. Recognize the two layers of ignorance: what you know you don't know and what you don't even realize you don't know. Avoid producing characters who have surface cultural markers but lack authentic underlying cultural assumptions. Always get a member of the culture to beta read your manuscript — either a trusted reader or a professional sensitivity reader — to provide critical feedback. Examples: Bad — The Education of Little Tree (strong surface details but authorial positionality undermines authenticity). Good — Lovecraft Country (white author successfully draws on deep cultural parallels with evident care).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge Intersectionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict characters as people with multiple, interacting identities (gender, race, class, sexuality, ability, etc.) rather than as single-axis representatives of a culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember that experiences differ across combinations of identities: an asian man's experience differs from an asian woman's; sexual orientation, class, and other axes alter lived experience. Use intersectionality to avoid flattening whole groups into a single behavior or stereotype and to create more realistic, individual characters. Anti-pattern: treating members of a culture as all alike; example of bad handling — Babylon 5's 'Parliament of Dreams' implying other species lack intra-group variety. Example of good handling — Care Of by Ivan Coyote (demonstrates diverse lived experiences through intersectional lenses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make Certain They Are People (Person-First Characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray diverse characters as fully realized human beings with their own desires, priorities, and internal lives, not merely as tokens or plot devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center characters as if they were the protagonist of their own story; avoid using side characters only to further the protagonist's arc (which makes them feel less human). Ensure decisions, motivations, and agency are plausible and rooted in the character's own concerns, not only in service of the plot. This counters the 'un-personing' that underlies many forms of bigotry. Bad example: Kipling's 'Gunga Din' where the humanity of the Other is presented as a surprise. Good example: American War by Omar El Akkad (many characters across backgrounds feel human and psychologically complex).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Tokenism and Superficial Representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include diverse characters only as symbolic representation or to make a roster look demographically varied without substantive individualization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superficial 'palette' diversity — adding characters with only the most surface-level traits (name, skin color) — is meaningless and can be harmful. If you include a variety of people for its own sake, be sure to develop more than superficial traits and to give each person interiority and distinct agency. This criterion is treated as a specific anti-pattern and is addressed through the other recommendations (lead with why, research, person-first depiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Sensitivity Readers / Beta Readers from the Culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain feedback from people who share the identity or cultural background you are depicting to catch mistakes, stereotypes, and blind spots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensitivity readers can be professional or knowledgeable trusted friends; they are vital for reviewing tone, context, nuance, and potential harms. This is presented as a near-essential final check after research and revision. The article stresses this kind of feedback is 'absolutely vital' to ensuring accuracy and appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalize Diversity Through Worldbuilding When Appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: In settings where plausible, write worlds in which diverse demographic details are ordinary and not the focal point of characterization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science fiction and fantasy often allow authors to normalize diversity as incidental detail, treating demographic attributes like other descriptive elements. This can reduce the risk of exoticizing or stereotyping characters. However, in realistic/real-world settings, normalizing diversity requires accurate representation and awareness of local demographics and norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Open to Change and Evolving Norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that standards for appropriate representation evolve; remain flexible, receptive to critique, and willing to revise past assumptions or works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes there are no hard-and-fast universal rules and that what was acceptable in the past may no longer be a good model. Authors should apply guidance with humility, listen to feedback, and be willing to change writing practices and revise work as understanding and cultural norms shift.
